## Example 1.3(a) {#dc1-example-1-3-rewrite .dc-lesson}

<p>Consider the function <span data-math="y=a^x"></span> where <span data-math="a"></span> is a constant and <span data-math="a>0"></span>.</p>
<p class="dc-prompt"><strong>a)</strong> Using the identity <span data-math="a=e^{\ln a}"></span>, rewrite <span data-math="a^x"></span> as an exponential function with base <span data-math="e"></span>.</p>
<div class="dc-working fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><div aria-live="polite"><div class="dc-step"><p class="dc-step-label">Replace the base with an equal expression.</p><span data-math="a^x=\left(e^{{\color{#b55224}\ln a}}\right)^x"></span></div><div class="dc-step"><p class="dc-step-label">Use the power-of-a-power index law.</p><span data-math="\left(e^{{\color{#b55224}\ln a}}\right)^x=e^{x{\color{#b55224}\ln a}}"></span></div></div></div><p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 3 · Example 1.3(a)</p>

::: notes
One press of Next reveals the complete conversion as a single chunk; Previous hides the whole chunk. Ask students to attempt the conversion, then justify both equalities using an inverse identity and an index law. Orange identifies the same constant ln a in every line. a>0 ensures ln a is defined. Even a=1 is allowed: it gives the constant function 1. This is an equivalent expression for the same function, not an approximation or a change of function. Follow-up: “We now have base e. What is the derivative of its exponent?” Answers remain hidden until deliberately revealed. After the working is shown, the next press of Next advances to the next slide.
:::
